screens.title: vEdge versus cEdge
screens.narratorSegment: Let's compare the two edge router families so you can pick the right device for each deployment. vEdge devices are Cisco's purpose‑built SD‑WAN appliances or virtual machines that run the Viptela OS directly. They are designed for SD‑WAN workloads from the ground up. cEdge devices are existing ISR or ASR platforms running IOS XE with SD‑WAN features; they let you reuse hardware in branches or data centers. Practically, this means their CLIs differ: vEdge uses Viptela OS commands and workflows while cEdge uses IOS XE commands for SD‑WAN operations. For example, a site with many existing ISRs can often convert them into cEdge routers by installing the IOS XE SD‑WAN software, saving hardware costs. Conversely, if you need a virtual edge in a cloud deployment you might choose a vEdge Cloud instance. A common misconception is thinking their role in the fabric changes; it does not. Both forward user traffic and participate in OMP, but knowing the OS differences matters for ticketing, debugging, and CLI command names. Check your team's operational familiarity and upgrade cycle before choosing. Which family aligns best with your existing inventory and skill set?

Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › vEdge vs cEdge
vEdge Routers
Purpose‑built appliances or virtual instances running Viptela OS. Common for new SD‑WAN deployments and cloud edge instances.
  • Runs Viptela OS and Viptela CLI conventions.
  • Often delivered as physical models or cloud VMs (vEdge Cloud).
  • CSR and certificate commands follow the vEdge CLI syntax.
Note: choose vEdge for greenfield or cloud‑native deployments.
cEdge Routers
Existing ISR/ASR platforms running IOS XE SD‑WAN. Ideal for reusing branch routers and applying SD‑WAN features on familiar hardware.
  • Runs IOS XE SD‑WAN; CLI and command names differ from Viptela OS.
  • Can be converted from existing ISR/ASR routers by installing SD‑WAN software.
  • Manual onboarding commands use the cEdge CLI syntax.
Note: choose cEdge to leverage existing inventory and operational experience.
Both types perform the same fabric functions: control plane, data forwarding, and OMP participation.
Misconception: Difference affects fabric role. Reality: only the OS and CLI differ; the overlay behavior is consistent.
Practical tip: align device family choice with staffing skills and hardware lifecycle plans.

screens.title: Zero‑Touch Provisioning (ZTP) Workflow
screens.narratorSegment: Zero‑Touch Provisioning lets devices join a fabric automatically when prerequisites are met. The workflow begins when a new vEdge or cEdge boots and obtains an IP address via DHCP. Next, the device resolves the vendor ZTP host name — for vEdge it uses the Viptela ZTP host, and for cEdge it uses the Cisco ZTP host. The ZTP server then validates the device using its serial number against the organization's Smart Account and Plug and Play listing. If validation succeeds, the ZTP service returns the IP address of your vBond orchestrator. The edge device then initiates a control connection to vBond; vBond authenticates the device and directs it to vManage and vSmart so the controllers can exchange keys and policies. Finally, vManage pushes the device template and full configuration. A common failure point is inability to resolve the ZTP host, which prevents the sequence entirely. For ZTP to work you must have the device registered in your Smart Account, DHCP available for initial addressing, and internet or DNS access to reach the ZTP host. When these conditions are satisfied, ZTP scales onboarding across hundreds of sites with minimal manual configuration.

keyIdea.title: ZTP in brief
keyIdea.text: DHCP → ZTP host resolution → serial validation → vBond IP returned → device connects and is configured by vManage.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Zero‑Touch Provisioning
ZTP Sequence
  1. Device boots and gets IP via DHCP.
  2. It resolves the ZTP host and contacts the ZTP server.
  3. ZTP validates the serial number against Plug and Play/Smart Account.
  4. ZTP returns the organization's vBond IP address on success.
  5. Device connects to vBond; vBond authenticates and points to vManage and vSmart.
  6. vManage pushes templates and configuration; device becomes operational.
Prerequisites: device must be registered in Smart Account, have DHCP and DNS reachability, and permit outbound connections to the ZTP host.
Quick checks
  • Verify DHCP is handing an IP.
  • Confirm DNS resolves the ZTP host name.
  • Ensure the device's serial number is registered in your Smart Account.
  • Confirm outbound firewall rules allow contact with the ZTP service.
Why it matters: if any step fails, the device never reaches vBond and the automated onboarding halts.

screens.title: ZTP Prerequisites and Validation
screens.narratorSegment: Before relying on ZTP, confirm three core prerequisites. First, the device's serial number must be registered in your Cisco Smart Account and synchronized with vManage. Without that registration, the ZTP server cannot validate the device and will not return your vBond address. Second, the device needs basic network services: DHCP to receive an initial IP and DNS or direct host resolution so it can find the vendor ZTP host. A technician should verify that the device can resolve the ZTP host name and reach it over the network before assuming ZTP will proceed. Third, the environment must allow outbound connectivity to the ZTP service and ultimately to your vBond orchestrator. Firewalls or NAT rules that block these outbound connections will stop onboarding. A common misconception is that ZTP alone ensures security; in reality, ZTP only automates discovery — mutual authentication still depends on certificates and CA trust once the controllers take over. Verify these prerequisites in advance to avoid troubleshooting remote branch failures. ZTP Prerequisites and Validation means registered serial, dhcp + dns connectivity, and allowed outbound connectivity to ztp and vbond.. In practical terms, what must be in place before a device can use zero‑touch provisioning. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › ZTP Prerequisites
Registration
Ensure the device serial is present in your Smart Account and visible to vManage for validation.
Why this matters
The ZTP server uses the serial number to map the incoming device to your organization. Without it, ZTP will not hand out the vBond address.
Network services
DHCP for initial IP; DNS resolution to find the ZTP host; and firewall policies allowing outbound reachability.
Practical test
Verify DHCP lease, run an upstream DNS query for the ZTP host, and confirm firewall allows outbound on required ports.
Misconception check
ZTP only automates addressing and discovery. Security and trust depend on certificates and controller CA trust. Register devices and ensure CA consistency across controllers and edges.

screens.title: Common ZTP Failures and Quick Fixes
screens.narratorSegment: When ZTP fails, the most immediate check is basic connectivity and DNS resolution. If a device cannot resolve the vendor ZTP host, it will never start the validation step. A technician should first confirm DHCP assigned an address and that DNS queries for the ZTP host return an address. If DNS fails, fix name resolution or add a temporary host entry in lab scenarios. The next layer is serial registration: confirm the serial shown on the device matches the entry in your Smart Account and vManage. If not registered, add it and retry ZTP. Another frequent issue is firewall or NAT blocking outbound traffic to the ZTP server or to vBond; validate that outbound rules permit the device to reach public ZTP endpoints and the vBond IP returned by the service. Finally, if ZTP gives the vBond IP but control connections fail, shift to certificate and time checks — certificate CA mismatch and NTP drift are leading causes of later-stage failures. A disciplined checklist of DHCP, DNS, registration, firewall, and certificate/time checks usually resolves ZTP problems quickly. Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › ZTP Troubleshooting
Network checks
  • DHCP lease present? Verify the device has an IP.
  • DNS resolution for ZTP host successful?
  • Firewall/NAT allowing outbound traffic?
Inventory checks
  • Serial and chassis ID registered in Smart Account and synced to vManage.
  • Serial shown by device equals entry in vManage's WAN Edge List.
After vBond handed out
  • Certificate CA mismatch: ensure same CA signs controllers and devices.
  • NTP drift: verify time sync; certificate validation is time sensitive.
Common mistake: assuming vBond is the cause. Often the device never reached ZTP because of DNS or DHCP failures.

screens.title: Manual Onboarding: End‑to‑End Steps
screens.narratorSegment: Manual onboarding reproduces the secure identity exchange that ZTP automates. The process begins by generating a Certificate Signing Request on the device. For vEdge the command is the request sdwan control generate‑csr family, and for cEdge there is an analogous request platform software sdwan generate‑csr call. Copy the CSR and have it signed by the same CA that signed your controllers, then install the signed certificate on the device and ensure the root CA is present. Next, configure the vBond orchestrator IP on the edge device; this tells the node where to initiate its control connections. In vManage you perform a manual add: supply serial number, chassis ID, model, and the System IP you plan to assign. The System IP is the device's persistent overlay identifier used by OMP. Finally, push a device template or full configuration from vManage to bring the device online. Each step must match the certificate common name and the serial registration to avoid authentication failures. Practicing this sequence makes lab and production manual onboarding predictable and auditable. Manual Onboarding: End‑to‑End Steps means generate csr → sign with same ca → install certificate → configure vbond → add device in vmanage with system ip → push template.. In practical terms, from csr generation to pushing device templates in vmanage. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Manual Onboarding
Step sequence
  1. Generate CSR on device.
  2. Copy CSR and get it signed by the same CA as controllers.
  3. Install the signed certificate and root CA on device.
  4. Configure vBond IP on device.
  5. Manually add device in vManage with serial, chassis ID, and System IP.
  6. Push device template or full configuration.
Remember: the CSR must include the serial number and chassis ID so the CA signed certificate matches the device identity recorded in vManage.
Example commands (vEdge)
# config t
# request sdwan control generate-csr
# (copy output, get signed by CA)
# request sdwan control install-certificate
-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
MIIDZjCCAs6gAwIBAgIQD+... (truncated)
-----END CERTIFICATE-----
# system
#  controller vbond 192.0.2.10
# commit and-quit
Use the vManage UI to manually add the device and assign its System IP after certificate installation.

screens.title: Generating and Installing CSRs (vEdge & cEdge)
screens.narratorSegment: Certificates are central to establishing trust between edge devices and controllers. On vEdge you generate a CSR using the request sdwan control generate‑csr command; on cEdge the equivalent is request platform software sdwan generate‑csr. The CSR embeds the device serial and chassis ID so the Certificate Authority can issue a certificate tied to that hardware identity. After you obtain the signed certificate, install it back on the device with the install‑certificate command appropriate to the platform. You must also ensure the root CA used to sign the controllers is installed on the device. A common mistake is installing a certificate signed by a different CA than the controllers; this causes mutual authentication failure even if the CSR and serial match. To verify, use show control local‑properties or show sdwan control connections to inspect certificate details and connection states. Practice the exact command sequences in the code examples, and after installation check the certificate subject and CA chain. This concrete verification step is what saves hours during live onboarding. screens.title: Configuring vBond and System IP
screens.narratorSegment: Two configuration items are essential after certificate installation: the vBond orchestrator IP and the System IP. The vBond IP tells the edge device where to initiate control plane authentication. Without the correct vBond IP configured on the device, the node cannot reach the orchestrator to exchange credentials and will not be directed to vManage and vSmart. Configure the vBond address using platform syntax — for vEdge under system controller vbond and for cEdge under sdwan controller vbond. The System IP is a stable, loopback‑style address that acts as the device's identifier inside the overlay and is used by OMP and BGP. Assign a unique System IP when you add the device into vManage's WAN Edge List; duplicates cause fabric instability. A common misconception is thinking the System IP is the physical interface IP; it is not. System IP must be unique and persistent across interface changes. screens.title: Common Onboarding Issues and Remedies
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting onboarding requires targeted checks for the usual suspects. Certificate mismatches are the most frequent problem: ensure the device certificate is signed by the same CA as controllers and that the certificate's common name matches the device serial. Verify by inspecting certificate subject on the device and the entry in vManage. Connectivity problems are next: confirm the device can reach vBond and that firewall or NAT rules do not block outbound control traffic. Use ping and traceroute or simple reachability checks to locate network blocks. Time synchronization is another silent killer — if the device clock diverges from the controllers, certificate validation will fail; check NTP status and sync. Serial number and chassis ID typos in vManage prevent attachment; always copy the identifiers directly from show hardware inventory or control local‑properties. Finally, avoid System IP duplication: assign and track System IPs centrally and verify uniqueness before pushing templates. When a control connection shows certificate errors, inspect the CA chain and the certificate CN first, then check NTP, and only after those checks move to routing or access lists. A methodical ordering of checks minimizes time to resolution.

fullNarratorScript:
In this module you'll learn how to bring edge routers into a Cisco SD‑WAN fabric reliably. We focus on two device families — vEdge appliances and cEdge routers — explain the automated Zero‑Touch Provisioning process that scales deployments, and step through manual onboarding when automation is not possible. You'll see why serial numbers, chassis IDs, and the System IP matter for identity and routing, and how certificates and time synchronization underpin secure control connections. Together, these topics let you deploy new branch and cloud routers without surprises. For example, you will understand why a device that cannot resolve the ZTP host never begins onboarding, and why a certificate signed by a different CA will cause control connections to fail. By the end you will be able to choose ZTP or manual onboarding appropriately, run the necessary CLI commands to generate and install certificates, and apply practical checks to resolve common failures. Keep an eye out for the step sequences and command patterns shown — they are the exact workflow you will practice in the hands‑on activity.

First, you'll be able to distinguish vEdge and cEdge routers by their platform and management style. Understanding that vEdge runs the Viptela operating system while cEdge runs IOS XE SD‑WAN explains why their CLIs and upgrade paths differ, and it helps you plan migrations when you have existing ISR/ASR hardware. Second, you'll learn the Zero‑Touch Provisioning workflow end to end: how a device gets an IP, reaches the ZTP host, and receives the vBond orchestrator address. This knowledge helps you scale branch deployments and spot early failures. Third, you'll practice manual onboarding steps, generating and installing certificate requests, configuring the vBond IP, and attaching devices in vManage. These are the exact steps you'll run in lab and production when ZTP is unavailable. Fourth, you'll learn to diagnose common problems: certificate mismatches, DNS failures, NTP issues, serial/chassis misentries, and System IP duplication. Together, these objectives will let you bring devices into the fabric with confidence and repair failed connections quickly.

This continuation emphasizes the 'why' behind the tasks. You will learn why the System IP is more than a label — it acts as the overlay router ID used by OMP and must be unique across the fabric. You will practice matching serial numbers and chassis IDs between device output and the vManage entry, because even small typos prevent device attachment. Finally, you'll gain the troubleshooting habit of verifying DNS resolution, NTP synchronization, and CA consistency before assuming complex faults. For example, when an edge device shows a certificate error, the two most common root causes are a mismatched CA or wrong common name tied to the serial number. A methodical checklist — DNS, connectivity to vBond, certificates, and time — lets you resolve most onboarding failures quickly. These objectives make the difference between slow rollouts and predictable, repeatable deployments.

Let's compare the two edge router families so you can pick the right device for each deployment. vEdge devices are Cisco's purpose‑built SD‑WAN appliances or virtual machines that run the Viptela OS directly. They are designed for SD‑WAN workloads from the ground up. cEdge devices are existing ISR or ASR platforms running IOS XE with SD‑WAN features; they let you reuse hardware in branches or data centers. Practically, this means their CLIs differ: vEdge uses Viptela OS commands and workflows while cEdge uses IOS XE commands for SD‑WAN operations. For example, a site with many existing ISRs can often convert them into cEdge routers by installing the IOS XE SD‑WAN software, saving hardware costs. Conversely, if you need a virtual edge in a cloud deployment you might choose a vEdge Cloud instance. A common misconception is thinking their role in the fabric changes; it does not. Both forward user traffic and participate in OMP, but knowing the OS differences matters for ticketing, debugging, and CLI command names. Check your team's operational familiarity and upgrade cycle before choosing. Which family aligns best with your existing inventory and skill set?

Zero‑Touch Provisioning lets devices join a fabric automatically when prerequisites are met. The workflow begins when a new vEdge or cEdge boots and obtains an IP address via DHCP. Next, the device resolves the vendor ZTP host name — for vEdge it uses the Viptela ZTP host, and for cEdge it uses the Cisco ZTP host. The ZTP server then validates the device using its serial number against the organization's Smart Account and Plug and Play listing. If validation succeeds, the ZTP service returns the IP address of your vBond orchestrator. The edge device then initiates a control connection to vBond; vBond authenticates the device and directs it to vManage and vSmart so the controllers can exchange keys and policies. Finally, vManage pushes the device template and full configuration. A common failure point is inability to resolve the ZTP host, which prevents the sequence entirely. For ZTP to work you must have the device registered in your Smart Account, DHCP available for initial addressing, and internet or DNS access to reach the ZTP host. When these conditions are satisfied, ZTP scales onboarding across hundreds of sites with minimal manual configuration.

Before relying on ZTP, confirm three core prerequisites. First, the device's serial number must be registered in your Cisco Smart Account and synchronized with vManage. Without that registration, the ZTP server cannot validate the device and will not return your vBond address. Second, the device needs basic network services: DHCP to receive an initial IP and DNS or direct host resolution so it can find the vendor ZTP host. A technician should verify that the device can resolve the ZTP host name and reach it over the network before assuming ZTP will proceed. Third, the environment must allow outbound connectivity to the ZTP service and ultimately to your vBond orchestrator. Firewalls or NAT rules that block these outbound connections will stop onboarding. A common misconception is that ZTP alone ensures security; in reality, ZTP only automates discovery — mutual authentication still depends on certificates and CA trust once the controllers take over. Verify these prerequisites in advance to avoid troubleshooting remote branch failures. ZTP Prerequisites and Validation means registered serial, dhcp + dns connectivity, and allowed outbound connectivity to ztp and vbond.. In practical terms, what must be in place before a device can use zero‑touch provisioning. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When ZTP fails, the most immediate check is basic connectivity and DNS resolution. If a device cannot resolve the vendor ZTP host, it will never start the validation step. A technician should first confirm DHCP assigned an address and that DNS queries for the ZTP host return an address. If DNS fails, fix name resolution or add a temporary host entry in lab scenarios. The next layer is serial registration: confirm the serial shown on the device matches the entry in your Smart Account and vManage. If not registered, add it and retry ZTP. Another frequent issue is firewall or NAT blocking outbound traffic to the ZTP server or to vBond; validate that outbound rules permit the device to reach public ZTP endpoints and the vBond IP returned by the service. Finally, if ZTP gives the vBond IP but control connections fail, shift to certificate and time checks — certificate CA mismatch and NTP drift are leading causes of later-stage failures. A disciplined checklist of DHCP, DNS, registration, firewall, and certificate/time checks usually resolves ZTP problems quickly. Finally, push a device template or full configuration from vManage to bring the device online. Each step must match the certificate common name and the serial registration to avoid authentication failures. Certificate mismatches are the most frequent problem: ensure the device certificate is signed by the same CA as controllers and that the certificate's common name matches the device serial. Verify by inspecting certificate subject on the device and the entry in vManage. Connectivity problems are next: confirm the device can reach vBond and that firewall or NAT rules do not block outbound control traffic. Use ping and traceroute or simple reachability checks to locate network blocks. Time synchronization is another silent killer — if the device clock diverges from the controllers, certificate validation will fail; check NTP status and sync. Serial number and chassis ID typos in vManage prevent attachment; always copy the identifiers directly from show hardware inventory or control local‑properties. Finally, avoid System IP duplication: assign and track System IPs centrally and verify uniqueness before pushing templates. When a control connection shows certificate errors, inspect the CA chain and the certificate CN first, then check NTP, and only after those checks move to routing or access lists. A methodical ordering of checks minimizes time to resolution.

These three compact concepts summarize the chapter. First, vEdge and cEdge are functionally equivalent within the SD‑WAN fabric but differ in operating system and CLI; choose based on hardware inventory and operational familiarity. Second, ZTP automates initial discovery by resolving a vendor ZTP host, validating the device serial against your Smart Account, and returning the vBond address; ensure DHCP, DNS, and registration are in place. Third, manual onboarding reproduces the secure identity exchange: generate a CSR, have it signed by the same CA as controllers, install the signed certificate and root CA, configure vBond and System IP, add the device in vManage, and push the template. Keep a troubleshooting order in mind: DNS and connectivity first, then certificate CA/CN and NTP, followed by identifier and System IP checks. A final set of compact reminders will help during real deployments. Serial numbers and chassis IDs are authoritative device identifiers used by ZTP and included in CSR common names, so copy them exactly from device output. The System IP is the overlay identifier used by OMP and must be unique; treat it as a registry entry you manage centrally. Certificates must be signed by the same CA that signed the controllers; a different CA causes mutual authentication failures even when all other settings are correct. Establish a short verification script for onboarding: check DHCP and DNS first, confirm serial registration, ensure CA chain consistency and NTP synchronization, set vBond and System IP, then add the device in vManage and push the template. This short checklist will become your fastest route to a successful onboarding and minimal downtime during branch rollouts.
